group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 52-year-old man with a background of ischemic cardiomyopathy complicated by chronic systolic dysfunction (most recent outpatient echocardiogram three months earlier showed an ejection fraction in the mid-30s) and a remote left parietal infarct that required a brief course of inpatient rehabilitation two years ago was transported to the emergency department by family after he awoke at dawn speaking incoherently, unable to recall the month, and insisting he was in a hotel rather than at home. According to his spouse, he had complained of progressive cough over the preceding five days, initially dry but now producing small amounts of yellow-green sputum, intermittent shaking chills, and a sensation of “burning” behind the sternum whenever he drew a deep breath. He normally works as an accountant from a home office, performs all activities of daily living independently, and has not been hospitalized in more than a year. His routine laboratory panels during cardiology and primary-care visits have consistently shown normal serum creatinine and stable liver transaminases. Home medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, low-dose furosemide only as needed for ankle swelling (none taken over the past week), aspirin 81 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly; he is a lifelong non-smoker, drinks two glasses of wine per week, and denies recreational drug use. He has no prior diagnosis of chronic kidney disease or liver disease, has never required dialysis, and denies any history of hepatitis, cirrhosis, or other hepatic disorders. He received an influenza vaccine in the autumn but has not yet obtained the current season’s pneumococcal booster. Emergency medical services reported that he was seated on the sofa when they arrived, answering questions slowly and misidentifying the day of the week, with no focal motor deficit or seizure activity en route; no intravenous line, oxygen, or medications were administered before arrival. In triage, prior to any antipyretics, fluids, or antimicrobial agents, vital signs were: oral temperature 38.1 °C, pulse 94 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 119/74 mm Hg with a palpable systolic of 119 mm Hg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute with quiet chest excursions, and pulse oximetry 92 % on ambient air. He appeared flushed and slightly diaphoretic, sitting upright but confused; he recognized his spouse but was unsure of the hospital name and answered only one of three orientation questions correctly. Mucous membranes were moist, sclerae anicteric, and no cervical adenopathy was palpable. Jugular venous contour was at the level of the clavicle at 45°, similar to baseline. Cardiac examination revealed a displaced point of maximal impulse and a soft third heart sound without new murmurs or pericardial rub. Lung auscultation disclosed diminished breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the right lower posterior zone; percussion was dull in the same area, and tactile fremitus was moderately increased, but there was no stony dullness or asymmetry of diaphragmatic excursion to suggest fluid accumulation. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge was not palpable. Extremities were warm with 2+ distal pulses and no peripheral edema or clubbing. Neurologic screening showed equal pupils, symmetric facial movements, 5/5 strength throughout, intact cerebellar finger-to-nose testing, but he was oriented only to person and exhibited short-term memory gaps, consistent with acute encephalopathy rather than residual stroke deficit. A finger-stick glucose measured 124 mg/dL. Venous blood draw and arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of arrival, before any therapeutic intervention. Initial laboratory results revealed hematocrit 30 %, white blood cell count 13.6 × 10⁹/L with 82 % neutrophils, serum sodium 145 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated pH 7.46, PaCO₂ 36 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 82 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, and an A-a gradient mildly above age-predicted norms. High-sensitivity troponin I was undetectable, lactate 1.5 mmol/L. A portable posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiograph obtained minutes later showed a dense alveolar opacity with air bronchograms localized to the right lower lobe; the diaphragmatic costophrenic angles were sharp, and there was no meniscus sign or shift of mediastinal structures. Cardiothoracic ratio was unchanged from an outpatient film six months prior, and pulmonary vasculature was not engorged. Electrocardiography displayed sinus rhythm at 92–94 beats per minute with left ventricular hypertrophy criteria and nonspecific ST-T changes but no acute ischemia. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and a rapid viral panel were sent while the patient remained on room air, seated upright, and he had not yet received intravenous crystalloids, diuretics, supplemental oxygen, or antibiotics at the time this note was completed.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points using admission values.
- Demographics: a 52-year-old man starts at 52 points. He lives at home: no nursing-home points.
- Comorbidities: chronic systolic heart failure +10; prior stroke (cerebrovascular disease) +10. No malignancy, liver disease, or renal disease is reported: +0.
- Examination: new disorientation to place and time qualifies as altered mental status: +20. Respiratory rate 15 (<30), systolic BP 119 (≥90), temperature 38.1°C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 94 (<125) each score 0.
- Laboratory findings: pH 7.46 (≥7.35), BUN 16 mg/dL (<30), sodium 145 mEq/L (≥130), glucose 124 mg/dL (<250), and PaO₂ 82 mmHg (≥60) each score 0. Hematocrit is exactly 30%, not below 30%: 0.
- Radiograph: consolidation without pleural effusion: 0.
Total: 52 + 10 + 10 + 20 = 92 (risk class IV).
Final answer: 92
